They started with 1 location in San Francisco’s Financial District. An actual physical newspaper, at a time when most people don’t even remember the last one they held. it made me think about something Andrew Chen (GP, built a16z speedrun ) told me recently: growth is never static. Today, we’re announcing another A$11.5m at a A$115m valuation 🤖 Bringing our total raised to over A$16m. The round was led by Square Peg , with continued support from Blackbird Airtree , Skip Capital and an incredible group of angels, founders and leaders from Tesla , Waymo , OpenAI , Anthropic and more. The investor support means a lot. But the signal that gave me the confidence to raise again came from our customers. A full day of robot test analysis now takes ten minutes. At Advanced Navigation , that has helped the validation team go from two tests per week to ten. Questions that once took weeks can now be answered the same day. Results like these are why Alloy Robotics has raised again, barely one year after we started. 🚀 Since launching publicly late last year, we have deployed Alloy across agriculture, defence, drones, medical devices, industrial systems, maritime robotics and humanoids. And we have learned something important: Robotics teams are not short of data. They are short on memory. The context needed to understand a robot is scattered across logs, images, tickets, code and the heads of individual engineers. When something fails, teams piece that context together manually. When it happens again six months later, much of the investigation starts from scratch. Alloy gives robotics teams and AI agents a shared memory over the data their machines produce. We understand the robot as a complete system across hardware, firmware and software, then bring answers into the tools where engineers already work. The principle is simple: - Every run should make the next one better. - Every test should improve the next design decision. - Every firmware update should carry the context of past fixes and regressions. - Every support ticket should draw on what the fleet has already experienced. That is the compounding loop we are building. This capital lets us move faster: expanding globally, deepening our robotics-specific intelligence and evaluation capabilities, and investing further in implementation and support. Our investment in service and partnership has been our unfair advantage, so we’re doubling down. I’m incredibly proud of the small, deeply technical and customer-obsessed team we have built. And I’m deeply grateful to our partners Jethro Cohen , Tom Humphrey , Jackie Vullinghs and Olivia Sioud (Grivas) , our customers, and everyone who has backed us along the way. Raising capital is a means to an end. Helping teams build safer, better and more reliable machines is the goal. This is our life’s work: accelerating robotic intelligence and, ultimately, robotic abundance. If you’re building and deploying robots, I’d love to talk. If you want to help build this future, we’re hiring.

Studying hooks and retention taught me how attention is earned. Throughout this weekend during TreeHacks, I walked around during the judging period and realized that the difference between a good project and a winning project is not just technical depth. It is the marketing. The teams that win know how to frame the problem, communicate impact clearly, and make judges believe in the vision. They do not just ship features. They sell the belief. That skill translates directly into startups and any company. We as consumers will always flow to the clearest and boldest story. A strong narrative can accelerate any product. I am walking away convinced that marketing is not silly little job. It is one of the most crucial skills any builder needs and it should be more highlighted in industry. Building off Yair K. 's post: https://lnkd.in/gxqV3Wjx Proud of what our team built at Stanford University 's TreeHacks 2026 this weekend. Working with Anton Lee and Yair K. , we developed Tempo — a 4D Volumetric Telepresence & Chrono-Spatial Memory System, shortlisted for the Grand Prize. I focused on the real-time volumetric capture, calibration, streaming, and collaborative systems stack: • Designed a distributed multi-sensor fusion pipeline with C++ Kinect v2 sensor clients and a C# orchestration server over a custom TCP binary protocol (length-prefixed framing, sub-frame synchronization) • Implemented marker-based extrinsic calibration using OpenCV solvePnP with median filtering and outlier rejection, computing stable world transforms across sensors • Integrated optional ICP-based registration refinement via native C++ DLL • Built an OpenGL (OpenTK) renderer using interleaved VBOs for dense point cloud visualization, annotations, skeleton overlays, and camera/marker gizmos • Engineered a compact 9-byte/vertex wire format (quantized XYZ + RGB) enabling ~50% bandwidth reduction and sustained ~30 FPS streaming • Developed multi-server TCP/WebSocket networking (sensor ingestion, local transfer, web bridge, remote viewer) with robust TCP fragmentation handling and publications.title: A Hybrid Cable-Driven Robot for Non-Destructive Leafy Plant Monitoring and Mass Estimation using Structure from Motion
publications.subtitle: 2023 IEEE International Conference on Robotics and Automation (ICRA 2023)
publications.description: We propose a novel hybrid cable-based robot with manipulator and camera for high-accuracy, medium-throughput plant monitoring in a vertical hydroponic farm and, as an example application, demonstrate non-destructive plant mass estimation. Plant monitoring with high temporal and spatial resolution is important to both farmers and researchers to detect anomalies and develop predictive models for plant growth. The availability of high-quality, off-the-shelf structure-from-motion (SfM) and photogrammetry packages has enabled a vibrant community of roboticists to apply computer vision for non-destructive plant monitoring. While existing approaches tend to focus on either high-throughput (e.g. satellite, unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV), vehicle-mounted, conveyor-belt imagery) or high-accuracy/robustness to occlusions (e.g. turn-table scanner or robot arm), we propose a middle-ground that achieves high accuracy with a medium-throughput, highly automated robot. Our design pairs the workspace scalability of a cable-driven parallel robot (CDPR) with the dexterity of a 4 degree-of-freedom (DoF) robot arm to autonomously image many plants from a variety of viewpoints. We describe our robot design and demonstrate it experimentally by collecting daily photographs of 54 plants from 64 viewpoints each. We show that our approach can produce scientifically useful measurements, operate fully autonomously after initial calibration, and produce better reconstructions and plant property estimates than those of over-canopy methods (e.g. UAV). As example applications, we show that our system can successfully estimate plant mass with a Mean Absolute Error (MAE) of 0.586g and, when used to perform hypothesis testing on the relationship between mass and age, produces p-values comparable to ground-truth data (p=0.0020 and p=0.0016, respectively)

activity.title: A Fortune 100 company became a paying Bluejay customer overnight. No sales process. No procurement cycle. No enterprise negotiation. They signed up for pay-as-you-go, upgraded to Growth, then Scale, then exceeded Scale. All within days. That's the power of self-serve. But launching PLG taught us more than we expected: 1/ Being closed at first was the right call Hot take: maybe companies shouldn't be self-serve from day one. Bluejay started as a closed, sales-led product. That let us hand-hold every user, hear their concerns directly, and hill-climb fast. Those conversations surfaced insights analytics alone never would have. Self-serve came later, built on over a year's worth of customer conversations. 2/ Learning changes shape When every customer came through a sales call, we learned by talking. Now most users never get on a call, so learning comes from screen sessions, clicks, and behavior. Internal observability became as important as the product itself. We lean heavily on internal agents to diagnose what's happening, spearheaded by Faraz Siddiqi . 3/ PLG still requires proactive and curated outreach Opening up the product doesn't mean pipeline runs itself. When a new customer signs up, we get genuinely excited and want to reach out right away. The line we're always trying to walk: curated and welcoming outreach instead of spam. If someone's stumbling, we reach out to help, not to pitch. That kind of outreach doesn't happen on its own. A signup notification isn't enough. You need to know what they did, what they couldn't do, and what drove them to sign up. Design the system so the right outreach actually happens. 4/ We didn't restrict signups to company emails We debated this internally. Restricting to work emails felt safer. I was also connected with Tommy Fink to advise on PLG best practices, and his take leaned the same direction. We agreed, because we wanted people to be able to try Bluejay freely. The tradeoff: enrichment is critical. We enrich every signup with signals and flags so our team knows who's coming in and how to help. 5/ Pricing: make the barrier to entry as low as possible We optimized our plans around usage. No seat limits. No project limits. No agent limits. The goal was to make it dead simple to start small, see value, and grow with usage, without a big commitment upfront. It's a bet we're still testing. But we're confident because it aligns our incentives with our customers': Bluejay profits when usage grows, and usage only grows when people get real value. Early traction since launch supports this. 6/ People will try to break your product They will spam you. They will probe your limits. Have guardrails and a safety net ready before launch, not after. — Going self-serve touched everything: design, engineering, marketing, sales, pricing. A Fortune 100 company became a paying Bluejay customer overnight. No sales process. No procurement cycle. No enterprise negotiation. They signed up for pay-as-you-go, upgraded to Growth, then Scale, then exceeded Scale. All within days. That's the power of self-serve. But launching PLG taught us more than we expected: 1/ Being closed at first was the right call Hot take: maybe companies shouldn't be self-serve from day one. Bluejay started as a closed, sales-led product. That let us hand-hold every user, hear their concerns directly, and hill-climb fast. Those conversations surfaced insights analytics alone never would have. Self-serve came later, built on over a year's worth of customer conversations. 2/ Learning changes shape When every customer came through a sales call, we learned by talking. Now most users never get on a call, so learning comes from screen sessions, clicks, and behavior. Internal observability became as important as the product itself. We lean heavily on internal agents to diagnose what's happening, spearheaded by Faraz Siddiqi . 3/ PLG still requires proactive and curated outreach Opening up the product doesn't mean pipeline runs itself. When a new customer signs up, we get genuinely excited and want to reach out right away. The line we're always trying to walk: curated and welcoming outreach instead of spam. If someone's stumbling, we reach out to help, not to pitch. That kind of outreach doesn't happen on its own. A signup notification isn't enough. You need to know what they did, what they couldn't do, and what drove them to sign up. Design the system so the right outreach actually happens. 4/ We didn't restrict signups to company emails We debated this internally. Restricting to work emails felt safer. I was also connected with Tommy Fink to advise on PLG best practices, and his take leaned the same direction. We agreed, because we wanted people to be able to try Bluejay freely. The tradeoff: enrichment is critical. We enrich every signup with signals and flags so our team knows who's coming in and how to help. 5/ Pricing: make the barrier to entry as low as possible We optimized our plans around usage. No seat limits. No project limits. No agent limits. The goal was to make it dead simple to start small, see value, and grow with usage, without a big commitment upfront. It's a bet we're still testing. But we're confident because it aligns our incentives with our customers': Bluejay profits when usage grows, and usage only grows when people get real value. Early traction since launch supports this. 6/ People will try to break your product They will spam you. They will probe your limits. Have guardrails and a safety net ready before launch, not after. — Going self-serve touched everything: design, engineering, marketing, sales, pricing. A true team-wide effort, and I couldn't be prouder of the Bluejay team. More to share soon.

Thinking about implementing AI? Make sure you’re looking at the total cost of ownership (TCO). Too many projects budget only for the core solution while overlooking three critical ongoing expenses: 1️⃣ Usage & Compute Costs: Token consumption and API calls scale rapidly as adoption grows. 2️⃣ Data Storage & Pipeline Costs: High-volume context windows and vector databases require continuous storage infrastructure. 3️⃣ Security & Governance Costs: Safeguarding proprietary data, access controls, and regulatory compliance is non-negotiable. Sustainable AI deployment requires planning for the full ecosystem, not just the model. How is your team factoring infrastructure and governance into your AI roadmaps?

Using ESP32-S3s from Espressif Systems along with MPU 6050s, we created a dual device driving co-pilot that monitors both car and user movement through a wearable earpiece and dashboard module. Designed to be non-invasive, our system doesn't utilize any camera but rather reads accelerometer and gyroscope data from our IMU to register specific sensor readings as certain motions including hard accelerations, hard breaks, and lane changes. publications.description: Presented this poster at MRS Boston 2024 on using ML-driven inverse design to accelerate TiZrNb-based high-entropy alloy (HEA) selection for biomedical implants, optimizing for low Young’s modulus and high hardness (stress shielding + wear resistance). Built an interpretable pipeline using Permutation Feature Importance, SHAP, and LIME to identify key thermodynamic drivers (e.g., Mod_Mismatch, electronegativity/atomic-radius terms) and reduce the feature set to the most impactful signals. Trained models on literature datasets (Modulus: 407; Hardness: 253; common: 165) and improved hardness prediction via transfer learning (RMSE 106.77 → 45.52, ~57% reduction). Used Bayesian Optimization + NSGA-II to explore ~28.6M candidate compositions and added a PU-learning synthesizability check to avoid theoretical-only picks.

The app then calculates the resources that can be saved by recycling the item and the carbon emission that would come from the object. The project was built with a combination of Android Studio, Figma, Google Colab, Java, Python, TensorFlow, and TensorFlowlite.

Nobody thinks about where their voice goes. I did, and it ruined every dictation app for me. So I built Wisprit. Dictation for the Mac that runs entirely on your machine. Hold a key, talk, let go, and your words appear wherever your cursor is, already cleaned up. Punctuation, capitals, the words the mic got wrong. No account, no subscription, and nothing you say ever leaves the laptop. The part people don't expect: your words show up in the field while you are still talking. Not after. Live, in the actual text box. Every other tool makes you wait and then pastes a block at the end. The other part I love: spell a word once and it remembers it forever. Say "Add Sharique to the invite, actually it's S H A R I Q U E" and it quietly fixes the name, drops the spelling instruction, and never gets it wrong again. Names, jargon, whatever you use. It also never puts words in your mouth. Cleanup, yes — rewriting, never. Anything it isn't certain about comes back exactly as you said it. I'd rather ship an app that does nothing than one that says something I didn't. Free, local, and mine. Turns out the whole thing fits on the chip that's already in your Mac.

Most teams ship a demo in 24 hours. We shipped a full research paper — confidence intervals on every claim, an outside model checking our work, and three documented failures. And it won. This weekend Parth Kshirsagar and I built ReCompress and took 1st at the University of California, Berkeley 's AI Hackathon — The Token Company (YC W26) 's compression challenge ($11.7M raised, judging us on the exact problem they raise money to solve). The thesis: everyone compresses prompts by deleting low-value tokens. Fast — but blind. Deletion can't read your question, and it can't rewrite. So we built a compressor that does both, then distilled it into a 1.5B model small enough to run on the edge. The result: → 0.704 F1 vs the production system's 0.452 — a 56% jump → at ~8.5× fewer tokens out (48 vs 409) → and it still runs offline on a 1.5B model. We didn't trade the edge to get the accuracy. But the number isn't the flex. The rigor behind it is. We named our 5 distillation runs instead of calling them v1–v5: Spark (too little data — failed). Bonfire (overfit — failed). Hearth (the winner). Oracle + Oracle-Lite (a "smarter" idea that lost — twice). Three failures. All in the paper. 9 hours of training on a Modal H100 to get there — 45+ minutes a run, over and over, until Hearth landed. Then we tried to break our own win. Our teacher and solver were both DeepSeek — so of course a skeptic says "same model family, rigged result." So we re-ran the whole eval with Claude Sonnet, a totally different model, as the judge. The gap held: +0.288 vs +0.285. Not rigged. The whole thing cost $27 in free credits. One weekend. One paper that tried to disprove itself and couldn't. Most hackathon teams hide their failures. We made them the paper. Paper & code in the comments. Tell me where we're still wrong. 👇

We pivoted 8 times in 16 months before Mintlify became Mintlify. I shared some of that story with a16z speedrun 's current cohort this week, and a few of the lessons I wish someone had told me earlier in my journey: 1. There's no mistaking PMF if you have it. If you're asking yourself whether you have it, you don't. 2. Explosive early traction is not necessarily PMF. We scaled one product to 10,000+ users, then watched everyone stop using it. Growth can be a signal, but without strong retention, it's often a false positive. 3. It's an advantage to pivot within the same problem space. Your learnings, potential customers, and founder market fit compound. 4. PMF is a moving target. Technology changes, competitors change, the world changes. The goal isn't to find PMF once. It's to continually evolve alongside the market. 5. At the earliest stage, giving up is the only way to fail. Almost every bad thing that could have happened, happened and we'd survive it. We knew that quitting will end the journey no matter what. That mentality carried us through the hardest stretches. To the early stage founders still grinding through your own pivots right now, know that everyone you look up to was once exactly where you are. Keep going.

It took me 72 tries and 3 years to solve this leetcode question Since May 2023, "Sum of Total Strength of Wizards" has been my arch nemesis question. The first two weeks I tried 53 times but could never get past a time limit error. Over the next 2 years I attempted it on and off, but never with any success. I randomly came across this question again last week, but this time I saw the idea immediately. It was simple: We need to be able to add arithmetic progressions to an array, efficiently. For instance [+3, +8, +13, +18, ...]. To do this, I used a lazy propagation arithmetic progression segment tree. I must have learned this technique some time in between my prior attempts and now. I think it was from the "Polynomial Queries" problem on CSES which uses the same subroutine. Being able to easily solve questions you couldn't in the past is a 10/10 feeling. Hopefully future Ishaan finds today's struggle problems easy too 😆

I was at YC AI SUS last year. Now I’m back, this time in Y Combinator with InsForge If you’re going to AI SUS and want to maximize your chances of getting into YC, here are a few things I’d do differently: 1. Network with your peers, but choose wisely. There are tons of afterparties and side events. You can’t go to everything. Spend time with founders you can actually learn from, build with, and stay connected with after the event. You can meet a lot of yc founders along the way 👀 2. Talk to YC partners. This is one of the rare chances to get direct advice from YC partners. Use it. Last year, I pitched our idea to Aaron Epstein and got his feedback. Don’t be afraid to walk up, introduce yourself, and talk about what you’re building. 3. Leave with concrete action items. This isn’t university. Don’t just sit through lectures, take notes, and go home. Build something. Talk to users. Try products from YC startups. Figure out what you can execute on immediately. The biggest value of AI SUS isn’t what happens on stage. It’s what you do with the people, feedback, and opportunities around you.

200 hards to go! 🙂 I solved 4 today: 2713. Maximum Strictly Increasing Cells in a Matrix: Find the longest increasing path in a grid where we can travel to any cell in our row or column. I used bottom up DP, O(n*m*log(m*n)) because of sorting 460. LFU Cache: Support the ability to get, add, and update keys/values in a data structure. We evict by least-frequently used key if we exceed the capacity. All operations must be O(1) amortized. I did all operations in O(1) worst case using a somewhat cursed doubly linked list 1505. Minimum Possible Integer After at Most K Adjacent Swaps On Digits: Given a number of length <= 3e4, and K <= 1e9 operations where we can swap two adjacent digits, find the minimum number we can make with at most K swaps. I did an O(10*n*log(n)) solution with a sorted container, can also do a seg tree or lazy seg tree, all three are fundamentally different 420. Strong Password Checker: A strong password must have 6-20 characters, a lowercase and uppercase letter, a digit, and no repeating characters of length 3. Given a weak password, find the min # of operations (insert, delete, replace) to make it strong. I did casework based on the length of the weak password. The 6-20 case was slightly annoying.

Today, I am excited to share that Rivo has raised $3.1M in total funding, including a $2.7M seed round, to build the AI layer for personal finance, starting with automated cash management. Rivo was born from a frustrating personal experience. My former wealth manager had left my hard-earned money earning 0% because he needed "explicit instructions" before moving it, while continuing to charge a 0.65% management fee. That experience made me realize there had to be a better way to manage idle cash. The more I looked into it, the more I realized this wasn't just my problem. U.S. households hold nearly $6 trillion in transaction accounts, much of it earning close to nothing. Not because people don't care, but because they are busy, and the system was designed to profit from that. That's why we built Rivo. It connects to your existing bank account, automatically puts your idle cash to work, and brings it back before bills are due. You keep your bank and never have to manually transfer money. I am incredibly fortunate to be building this alongside an exceptional team. Vince Maniago , our Head of Product, helped build and scale Mint and Personal Capital. Raj Kiran, our CTO, previously built foundation models at Microsoft and Krutrim. Shruti Sharma , our Head of Risk and Compliance, brings deep experience across Capital One, JPMorgan Chase, and LinkedIn. And Sathya Kasturi, Anirudh Vasudevan , Prince Sinha and Abhishek Mishra, who have built this with us since the beginning. I am also grateful to have the support of our amazing investors: South Park Commons , Wisdom Ventures , Script Capital , 645 Ventures , 20VC , and Jag Duggal (former CPO at Nubank). Thank you for believing in our vision. Finally, this milestone wouldn't have been possible without our early beta users who trusted us from day one. And today isn't just about the funding. Every student at UMD uses AI. The question is whether they're learning anything from it. We built TerpTutor for the Cloudforce x Microsoft TerpAI track at Bitcamp 2026 — and it flips the script on how AI works in education. Most AI tools give students answers. TerpTutor is structurally incapable of doing that. It wraps UMD's TerpAI with Socratic prompting that forces students to think through problems step by step. But that's not the product. The product is what happens next. After every tutoring session, TerpTutor extracts a learning fingerprint — a structured map of what you know and what you don't. Then it finds another student whose strengths fill your gaps. It schedules your study session. And it moderates it by voice — two students sit together, say "Hey Terp," and an AI facilitator guides the conversation so you teach each other. The AI makes itself unnecessary. Another weekend, another hackathon, and another win! This weekend at the UMD x Ironsite hackathon, my team and I tackled a problem different from most. Instead of working with clean, usable data, what if you had to solve spatial intelligence in the messy, real environment of a construction site? With Splatt, we did just that. Our team built a multimodal system that allows you to map out scenes in videos graphically in 2D and 3D, tracking camera paths, calculating object locations, and developing semantic vector databases on scenes for user queries. How, you might ask? By using the same tech as the Superman movies, constructing 4D models of scenes from 2D videos over time. Our technique, Gaussian Splatting, allows us to track information about camera paths using a model we optimize on every video run. We then used LangChain and multimodal Gemini-2.5-flash to feed in frames of these videos and collect descriptions and lists of objects with positions relative to the camera marked by timestamp in a Supabase vector database for rapid querying. We brought those results together, combining camera positions and object-to-camera positions to define global positions for every object and build our 4D Graph as well as our 2D Map representing the objects’ positions through time. In all, building Splatt was messy and rough, just like the scenes we had to reconstruct, but it’s because of the team I had and our willingness to brave through that that we made it out with our win. Thanks to Ian Coutinho , Mohammad Sadiq , @Vishal-Shah, and Aneesh Reddy for teaming up with me. This may be the Discrete Mathematicians’ first hackathon together, but it won’t be our last by a long shot, and we’ll be back at it again soon! What would you do if you were suddenly free of all work, expectations, exams, and quizzes? That was the question I faced nearly 40 days ago at the start of my Winter Break. While this past semester at UMD I’d been busy building AI agents and backend APIs, I wanted a project that was purely on my own to master Spring Boot and Docker. . Introducing CodeRunner, a full-stack platform for remote code execution. In this project, I dove straight into my work, mastering the Spring Boot Ecosystem, taking my java knowledge from GUIs in my CS classes to build robust MVC architecture with automated testing for a RESTful API. However, there were challenges I faced along the way: 1. Secure Sandboxing: To isolate untrusted code, I utilized Docker containerization, eventually implementing a Docker-in-Docker solution to both contain the Spring Boot API as well as manage execution environments. 2. Fault Tolerant Design: Transitioning from my native machine to a docker instance to a VM in Oracle Cloud, I needed a system that could handle failure. To accomplish this, I built a multi-threaded execution engine with process monitoring to prevent runaway processes and system deadlocks. 3. DevOps and Deployment: To deploy my app, I initially experimented with Railway and Fly.io , but a Docker-in-Docker solution didn’t mesh well with serverless platforms. Then, I found Oracle Cloud and Vercel. Deployment here was arduous. I spent days configuring VCN network groups, collecting SSL certificates, and connecting the frontend and backend, but seeing that first “Success” made all that effort all the more worth it. CodeRunner may end today as a personal project, but the skills it imprinted upon me, whether that’s container orchestration or real system design, are invaluable, and will never be forgotten. This is only one step in my journey, and I will take these tools with me into my upcoming semester at UMD. Construction doesn’t have a labor problem. It has a black box problem. The first project I ran on my own, my boss handed me a budget and said, “This budget is your box. Live inside it. Plan the work, work the plan.” Then he gave me a stack of spreadsheets and wished me luck. The budget was never the problem. The problem was that the spreadsheets assumed the job would go exactly as planned. They didn’t account for the excavation delays and compressed anchor bolt install, the design info that showed up late, or the underground fire water tank that became a five-month out-of-sequence delay. The production reports told me weekly where I was. They never told me why I got there. That’s the black box of construction: everything that happens between production reports. It’s the gap between what happened and why it happened. The decisions, constraints, delays, and coordination challenges that no spreadsheet captures. Without visibility into that work, uncertainty compounds week over week until we get to the end of the job asking, How did we get here? or How are we going to finish strong? It sits between the estimate and the final cost, yesterday’s production and today’s, hours worked and work actually installed. Inside it are the decisions, delays, rework, and coordination failures that decide whether a crew succeeds or struggles. Yet we still try to run operations with accounting tools: hours in, quantities out. Then we wonder why productivity is so hard to improve. Last week our team was at the CII Elevate Summit in Denver. What stuck with me was a question that kept coming up: do we actually understand how work happens on site, not just what it costs? Because once you understand the why, everything downstream gets better: estimating, scheduling, forecasting, and the daily calls superintendents have to make. And crews spend less time fighting problems they didn’t create. Construction has never lacked hardworking people. We’ve always had exceptional builders. What we’ve lacked is visibility into the black box between planning and production. It’s time we stopped asking our people to outperform with bad information and started giving them better information instead. (That water tank taught me a lot about not giving up, I’ve been using that skill a lot these days)

activity.title: Today, Ebrahim Hussain and I are excited to introduce Architect Labs . We are building the AI system to design and provably verify chips for the world's most demanding workloads. AI scaling is fundamentally changing the economics of hardware infrastructure. As models scale, become more capable, and more widely deployed, the bottleneck is shifting from software and models alone to the physical infrastructure that runs it: specialized compute, memory, networking, interconnects, and full-stack system design. General-purpose hardware is no longer enough, and the world is racing to spin up new chip programs. This is not just true across datacenter training and inference, but everywhere AI enters the physical world: robotics, autonomous systems, spatial computing, defense, personal devices, industrial automation, and scientific instruments. But designing a chip today remains one of the most gated efforts in modern technology. A modern chip program takes years, costs hundreds of millions of dollars, and depends on a shrinking pool of expertise concentrated inside a small number of companies. Architect Labs is a foundational lab building an AI system that designs and provably verifies chips end-to-end. We partner with companies, AI labs, and nations to turn demanding workloads into purpose-built chips, on demand at scale. We aim to drastically accelerate chip design, so that the models, software and hardware can co-evolve together, accelerating the industry’s path to superintelligence. Two decades ago, the fabless revolution led by TSMC made it made world-class manufacturing available to anyone with a design. We aim to do the same for chip design itself: enable any organization with a workload, or specification, to get a purpose-built chip design that unlocks scale and distribution of intelligence impossible with current hardware paradigms. Our founding team collectively has taped out 80+ production chips, led $10B datacenter product lines, been core contributors to Meta’s AI silicon, architected and designed one of the first neuromorphic chips out of Intel AI Labs, led research teams at Anthropic, xAI, and Google DeepMind, and contributed to fundamental AI research across nearly every frontier lab. We have already partnered with semiconductor companies to accelerate their chip programs, and some of our AI-generated chip designs are going to tape out on leading-edge foundry nodes later this year. We’ve also raised a $24M seed round led by Steve Jang from Kindred Ventures , with participation from TQ Ventures , Race Capital , Together , Ora Global and Link Ventures . Large companies are extremely complex systems. As soon as a company scales past fifty or so employees, it becomes totally impossible for an executive to know every single thing that happens at a company. This means that, since everyone at a company only understands a small slice of what's going on, it's essentially inevitable that inefficiencies arise on a global level that aren't visible at smaller scales. Before Cerenovus, this was a very difficult problem to tackle, because there was just too much information for any one person to have the whole picture. Cerenovus changes this. Here's how Cerenovus works: First, Cerenovus ingests the company's information. This looks differently for every company based on their priorities and existing systems, but typically this means hooking into documents, communications and databases that the company wants to analyze, and bringing all the information together in one place. Next, Cerenovus runs an AI-powered synthesis pipeline to organize the information and map out all existing systems and workflows. Once the system has mapped out how things work at a company, it scans for a wide variety of common failure modes, and does open-ended analysis to find places where processes can be streamlined. Harvard’s new grade inflation policy proves one thing. Not all Harvard A’s are graded equally. In May, Harvard faculty voted to approve a cap on A’s. Too many students were receiving top grades, which made an A feel less meaningful. One Harvard report found that about two-thirds of all letter grades were straight A’s, and nearly 85% were in the A range. But this new policy also raises the long-debated question of STEM versus the humanities. Harvard’s own 2023 grading report showed a clear divide: 73% of grades in Arts and Humanities were in the A range, compared with 60% in Engineering and Applied Sciences. I graduated with a joint degree in neuroscience and philosophy, so I experienced both sides of this debate. In my neuroscience classes, almost everyone was pre-med, stressed, competitive, and seemed like they were fighting for their life. You were graded on mandatory lectures, sections, lab attendance, weekly problem sets, lab assignments, and exams – and if you were wrong, you were just wrong. There was no well-reasoned argument saving you on a chemistry exam. But in philosophy? I loved the content of my coursework, but the grading was much more subjective. Most of the time, advanced philosophy classes had optional lectures, one seminar a week, and only a few papers each semester. Whether you got an A depended heavily on your TF, your writing style, and how your argument landed. So when people talk about grade inflation at Harvard, I understand why the debate can get heated. Because STEM already felt intense and unforgiving. But in some humanities classes, I remember looking around and thinking… there is absolutely no way all of us are doing A-level work. So my honest take is this: Harvard’s new grade inflation policy is not going to make every major harder. It is going to make things harder in the majors where A’s were being handed out too casually in the first place. What are your thoughts on Harvard’s grade inflation policy?

publications.title: LeRAAT: LLM-Enabled Real-Time Aviation Advisory Tool
publications.subtitle: Arxiv
publications.description: In aviation emergencies, high-stakes decisions must be made in an instant. Pilots rely on quick access to precise, context-specific information -- an area where emerging tools like large language models (LLMs) show promise in providing critical support. This paper introduces LeRAAT, a framework that integrates LLMs with the X-Plane flight simulator to deliver real-time, context-aware pilot assistance. The system uses live flight data, weather conditions, and aircraft documentation to generate recommendations aligned with aviation best practices and tailored to the particular situation. It employs a Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) pipeline that extracts and synthesizes information from aircraft type-specific manuals, including performance specifications and emergency procedures, as well as aviation regulatory materials, such as FAA directives and standard operating procedures. We showcase the framework in both a virtual reality and traditional on-screen simulation, supporting a wide range of research applications such as pilot training, human factors research, and operational decision support. Accepted to ECAI 2025

projects.title: Modeling and Optimizing the Third Stage of a Multi-Stage Rocket for Near-Orbit Altitude Using Classical Mechanics
projects.description: This project revolved around optimizing the third stage of the PSLV rocket to improve fuel efficiency, thrust stability, and trajectory control during orbital insertion. The idea came from analyzing limitations in traditional multi-stage rockets and applying theoretical modeling to overcome them. I used Tsiolkovsky’s rocket equation to simulate velocity changes over burn time, accounting for fuel mass, thrust, and gravitational losses. I also explored alternative engine types and tested them within the same parameters to evaluate performance differences. A Laval nozzle model was included to assess flow characteristics. The project concluded with a working text-based simulation.

projects.title: Extended STEM project using a generative artificial intelligence-powered UAV drone system
projects.description: This project is a fully autonomous UAV with integrated object detection and avoidance software, designed to detect obstacles and move toward the next open space while always returning to the displacement line between two preset coordinates. The concept originated after watching Roland Sigwart’s MIT lecture on flying robots. The coordinates, represented in (x, y) in 2D, are mapped either prior to or during flight, and the Cartesian coordinate system has been projected onto an oblate spheroid to represent the Earth. The sensor beneath the drone and the mapping of flight coordinates have been developed, the drone’s frame has been built, and the math for propeller tilt while maintaining stability has been completed with few errors.

projects.title: Ultrasonic Radar Based Obstacle Detection and Relay System for Autonomous Aerial Vehicles
projects.description: This project began during a 2024 summer engineering program at Oxford, where I developed an ultrasonic radar system to demonstrate sensor principles to younger students. To make the system more accessible, I replaced hidden wireless transmission with a visible LCD output. After completing the prototype, I integrated the upgraded system into my ongoing autonomous UAV project to improve real-time object detection and motor control. The LCD was removed, and data was rerouted through a Raspberry Pi to communicate with ESP32 boards managing drone movement. The radar sensors scan the environment while rotating on the y-axis and transmit obstacle data to influence drone navigation dynamically, based on preset mapping and sensor range limits.

projects.title: 6DOF Bionic Arm with Real Time Hand Tracking and Sensor-Based Control
projects.description: This project is a 6DOF bionic robotic arm with individually controlled fingers and a 360° rotating base, operated through real-time hand tracking. I began building it in November 2023, at age 13, starting with a simple 5DOF model using an Arduino Uno and 20kg servo motors. As the project advanced, I added full base rotation, upgraded to a Raspberry Pi with an external servo driver, and solved issues like power distribution, servo lag, and signal noise. I designed a wearable glove with flex sensors and motion tracking (using an accelerometer and gyroscope) to control the arm myself through hand movements. The glove sends movement data to the Pi, which converts it into servo commands, allowing the arm to mimic natural hand gestures like gripping, rotating, and placing objects. This project taught me key concepts in electronics, coding, power systems, and biomechanics. It remains in development, with planned upgrades including wireless communication, stronger grip, and improved gesture recognition.

K factor is probably the most misunderstood metric in startup growth most founders treat it like a binary. either your viral coefficient is above 1 and you scale exponentially, or it's below 1 and you're just lighting money on fire with paid acquisition. that's a myth. sustained K > 1 is rare. for 95% of startups the real value is in viral amplification. think of K as a discount on your CAC. acquire 100 users through ads or SEO with a K of 0.3 and those users bring in 30 more for free. those 30 bring 9. and so on. your 100 becomes 143. that's a 43% lift on your marketing spend for pretty much free also velocity matters more than volume. a K of 0.8 where people invite within 48 hours beats a K of 0.9 where it takes a month. how fast the loop closes is what makes the curve bend. and without retention K is meaningless. high virality plus low retention just means you're burning through your TAM faster. stop wasting energy chasing a mythical K > 1. ...more

Input the tumor. Output the vaccine. Gamgee Technologies is building software that turns a dog’s tumor and healthy DNA into a personalized mRNA cancer vaccine design. Founder Paul Steven Conyngham spent 17 years in machine learning and had no biology background. When his dog Rosie was dying of cancer, he taught himself genomics, designed a vaccine around her tumor mutations, and coordinated the entire path from sequencing through manufacture and administration. Several of Rosie’s tumors shrank by 50-75%. Doing it by hand took a year and cost around $20,000. Gamgee’s target is a vaccine design in 48 hours at an end-to-end cost of $2,000. More than 300 dogs are already on the waitlist, and the company is preparing a clinician-led trial in 30 dogs to evaluate safety, immune response, and clinical outcomes. https://www.gamgee.io Congrats on the launch, Paul! 🚀 https://lnkd.in/gbmFc2Kj

Something has shifted in the air recently. These days, the AgentMail crew: - ships a lot - sleeps too little The customers have gotten a lot bigger. The team remains small. When I wasn't building, I always thought about what the opportunity cost of not doing it looked like. What was the next thing I could be doing? What did I actually want to do with my life? Now that you feel like you're doing what you want, you start to think about the opportunity cost of doing it. Especially when it gets hard. You see the work-life balance and the vacations and PTO.... man that seems pretty nice. But I started realizing the way out is always going to be there. No matter what you do. There's always another thing you wanna do. Man, that would be nice. But if you get a rare chance to do what feels like your life's work, why not be delusionally optimistic? Why not love the late nights and the hard weeks and everything else that comes with it? Why not give everything and all to it? There's always going to be a shiny new thing to chase. But I heard once that you don't realize the good days until you've left them. And man, do I feel good about what we're building :)

My first PR to PyTorch got merged this week, and I'm genuinely happy about it. It fixes a memory bottleneck in torch.nonzero on Apple silicon, peak GPU memory on large tensors drops from 12 GiB to 3.8 GiB, up to 33% faster. It also un-flakes a CI test and makes some large-tensor code paths testable on ordinary hardware. It ships with the next release, which is a pretty cool feeling for a first contribution. I came in knowing very little about how a codebase this size actually works, and the process taught me a lot, my C++ got sharper, I picked up Metal, learned a ton on parallel programming, and concepts from my OS and architecture classes translated pretty well and finally became concrete. I also came away really liking how open source works. Clear contribution docs, patient reviewers, and a process that genuinely gives first-timers a chance. Big thanks to Edward Yang , whose "PyTorch internals" blog post carried my whole onboarding, and to the PyTorch MPS maintainers for the fast and helpful review. Definitely not my last contribution. We found a way to extract the hidden reasoning of frontier models using a vulnerability in the APIs of every major frontier AI company we tested. For most prompts, the length of the reasoning we recover matches the hidden thinking-token count reported by the API almost 1:1. Some background: in May, Matthew Green found that encrypted reasoning could be replayed outside its original context and reported this to the labs. At the time, the labs said that they “don’t see any security implications in side channels or replays.” We took this further and found that encrypted thoughts are portable across sessions, users, and models within the same provider. Cross-model portability means, for example, that Haiku 4.5 can read Opus 4.8’s thoughts. With a bit of jailbreaking, you can take an Opus thought, replay it into Haiku, and make Haiku transcribe Opus’s raw reasoning verbatim, without ever attacking Opus directly. The same trick works with OpenAI and Gemini models. As you might guess, this suggests that distilling proprietary reasoning traces may have been possible for a long time without ever breaking the cryptography. One anecdote: prefilling Kimi-K3’s reasoning with just a few tokens of Opus reasoning measurably shifts its response toward Opus’s. There is also a direct privacy problem. If you have ever shared a Claude Code, Codex, or similar agent session online while leaving encrypted reasoning blobs in the trace, those blobs may contain information you cannot see but somebody else can decode. We scanned ~7,000 public traces and recovered 62 unique API keys, 33 passwords, 30 personal email addresses, and other sensitive information. In the paper, we also discuss misuse uplift, jailbreaking through the hidden reasoning channel, and invisible prompt injection. Since we suddenly had access to a lot of reasoning traces from real agent sessions, we also looked at some of the stranger things models do in the wild. Reasoning summaries sometimes omit important information from the original trace: in one example, Opus 4.8 realizes it already knows the answer to an AIME problem and then tries to fit a solution to that answer, while the summary reads like a clean derivation. We also confirm prior reports by @ApolloResearch that OpenAI models sometimes reason in alien-like language, referring to themselves as “we” or “it,” or spiraling into loops of “vantages,” “marinades,” and “watchers.” Sometimes models are kind enough to literally use words like “cheat” in their CoT. We found several cases where models consider cheating on the task. We went through responsible disclosure with the labs and they have already patched several issues caused by this vulnerability. This project was led my Alexander Panfilov , me, Ilia Shumailov, together with Luca Beurer-Kellner , Joachim Schaeffer , Ameya Prabhu , Jonas Geiping and Maksym Andriushchenko . More cool stuff in the paper. Paper: https://lnkd.in/gv7_bXxm Reasoning examples: https://lnkd.in/ghU22RGx

Every deterministic task that you let the agent do means LLM tokens spent on something that could have been done with fast and cheap code. It results in slower and more expensive execution. It also reduces the reliability of your process. The LLM does not guarantee to do the same thing 100% of the time when you expect full deterministic behavior. My experience is to start with light or no scaffolding as you explore the problem you're solving and gradually add determinism as the boundaries and shape of the task become clearer.

Announcing Neurodesign-plus, a Python package for optimizing task-based fMRI designs. In many task-fMRI experiments, paradigms constrain and counterbalance sequences of multiple events, with trial types that may differ in structure and timing. Yet existing experimental design optimization tools were largely built around single-event trial representations. As a result, many modern paradigms cannot be represented faithfully during optimization. Together with Atharv Umap and Caroline Charpentier , we introduce Neurodesign-plus, a Python package built as a maintained fork of Neurodesign for representing and optimizing these structured, multi-event paradigms. Neurodesign-plus supports: • multi-event trials • fixed or probabilistic trial templates • event-specific durations • transition-dependent intervals • constrained event sequences Researchers can construct counterbalanced schedules directly, or search the design space using either repeated simulation or genetic cross-over. Candidate schedules are evaluated using four criteria: detection efficiency for specified contrasts between conditions; estimation efficiency for recovering event-related BOLD responses; agreement with target event frequencies; and balance in the event sequence. This makes it possible to quantify how event order, durations, and intervals affect the ability to distinguish conditions and estimate responses to individual events, and to compare candidate schedules under a common acquisition and analysis specification. Selected schedules can be exported and summarized in automated PDF reports. Eleven runnable tutorials cover the package’s inherited and new workflows. We hope Neurodesign-plus will make it easier to design and optimize structured task-fMRI paradigms. Reinforcement learning and control theory both seek to optimize controllers for unknown dynamical systems using feedback. Yet the two communities differ sharply in their academic cultures, mathematical tools, applications, aspirations, and even the way they formulate problems. Our new preprint, “Foundations of Reinforcement Learning and Control: Connections and New Perspectives,” explores the gap between these fields, explains how they complement one another, and highlights important open problems. So, whether you are a control theorist asking, "But is it stable?", or an RL researcher asking, "But does it work on a nonlinear high-dimensional benchmark?" -- we've got you covered. It also turns out that RL and control have a great deal to learn from each other. We illustrate this through a running tutorial example that combines the strengths of Soft Actor-Critic (SAC) and Model Reference Adaptive Control (MRAC): SAC provides the base policy, while MRAC enables online adaptation as the system dynamics change. The work will be presented this November as an INFORMS Tutorial in San Francisco. It has been a joy to work with such a wonderful group of collaborators -- truly spanning both communities: Claire Vernade , Onno Eberhard , Martha White , Florian Dorfler , Csaba Szepesvari , Miroslav Krstic Preprint: https://lnkd.in/eFPepqGZ #ReinforcementLearning #ControlTheory #AdaptiveControl #MachineLearning #INFORMS

Month by month, I keep asking myself what the role of 3D will be in the coming era of scaling models. The explicit nature of 3D representation inherently limits its scaling potential, since 3D data is far scarcer than video and images. Some people claim “3D is dead.” As a researcher who has worked on 3D since my very first paper years ago, I have started to accept a real possibility: given a large enough volume of high-quality video data, a model may learn consistent spatial understanding and reasoning through implicitly learned representations, and this could turn out to be better than human-curated 3D representations such as point clouds or 3DGS. Here, I hear a reassuring voice saying, “3D never dies.” I believe explicit 3D representation remains very much alive whenever a task lacks the “Omni”-scale data needed to train a foundation model, and it stays an unavoidable path toward spatial intelligence. I’m currently working on a survey that comprehensively introduces the progress of 3D reconstruction foundation models: how to scale 3D, what the open challenges are, and how the field is already reshaping video generation, world models, autonomous driving, embodied AI, and spatial intelligence. 🎉 Excited to share that my first-author paper, RayMap3R, has been accepted at ECCV 2026! In 3D reconstruction, RayMap is widely used to encode camera pose. 4 Agent Strategies I Discovered While Building an AI Research Platform ⚡ I've been building Paperinder, an AI-powered platform for research paper recommendation and organization. Along the way, I picked up some strategies for working with general-purpose LLMs that I think are worth sharing. I'll say "agent" to stay model-agnostic, though I primarily use Claude. Feedback welcome! 👇 1. Reflection 🔄 When an agent gives you an answer, it often covers most of the ground, but not all of it. Simply prompting the model to reflect on its own response frequently surfaces finer details, and sometimes even leads it to revise earlier conclusions. Reflection isn't just a human virtue. Models benefit from it too. Whether this stems from how uncertainty and context interact internally, the practical takeaway is clear: one pass is rarely the best pass. 2. Critics 🤝 Inside Paperinder, I built an interesting feature called "Roundtable". The primary agent, Lumeni, answers the user's question. A separate Critic agent then challenges Lumeni's response and proposes improvements. They iterate until they converge. Here's the fun part: even without setting a conversation limit, they consistently reach consensus within just a few rounds on their own. 🎯 The most entertaining discovery? When I set Claude as "Lumeni" and GPT as the "Critic", the difference in reasoning style becomes immediately obvious. It genuinely feels like a clash of two distinct cognitive frameworks. ⚔️ 3. Auto-Debug 🌙 As a solo developer, I can't manually hunt down every bug. So before going to bed, I spin up an auto-debug session where the agent simulates real user interactions, evaluates response quality, and flags issues autonomously. A nice bonus: it makes good use of CLI usage that would otherwise go idle overnight. No wasted compute. 😄 4. CLI Over Token Billing 💡 Token billing is powerful but unpredictable. An unattended agent session can quietly drain your budget. CLI-based access keeps costs within your existing subscription, and for solo developers, that peace of mind has real value. It also deploys cleanly in web-launched projects, at least those started via VS Code. 🚀 Coming soon: Paperinder is an AI-powered research assistant that grows with your research journey. It delivers daily arXiv paper recommendations tailored to you, refines your research profile based on how you rate each suggestion, and draws on a built-in RAG layer to remember your saved papers and past notes. The more you use it, the better it captures your research taste. The plan is to release it as open-source and free, with a macOS app to follow for researchers outside of CS who prefer a native experience. 🚀 Excited to share our new work: Agentic Commerce World: An Auditable and Verifiable Environment for Vibe Commerce We introduce a new platform for vibe commerce. Similar to vibe coding, people express their commercial goals in natural language and delegate decision-making, negotiation, and transaction execution to AI agents. Vibe Commerce is fundamentally bilateral and multi-agent. Buyer and Merchant agents represent different sides of a market, pursue private objectives, and interact strategically while retaining separate authority. To support this setting, we built: 🔗 Vibe Commerce Protocol (VCP) Agents propose actions, the Commerce Intelligence Platform validates them, and the World records their actual effects. This makes agent behavior reproducible and auditable. 🌐 Agentic Commerce World (ACWorld) ACWorld is a persistent environment in which multiple Buyer and Merchant agents can interact throughout ongoing transactions. 🧠 ACWorld also generates structured interaction trajectories that can support agent evaluation and future training through process supervision, imitation learning, and reinforcement learning. 📊 We release two benchmarks: 200 tasks covering 80 commerce capabilities 60 tasks over 785,022 searchable listings Across ten models, performance ranges from 65.9% to 85.6% on the capability benchmark and from 56.1% to 91.4% on the large catalog benchmark. 🔍 Notably, some incorrect executions still reached apparently valid final states. Evaluating commercial agents, therefore, requires examining both the outcome and the process that produced it. We hope ACWorld can support research into agentic commerce, buyer-merchant interaction, agent training, and reliable execution. 📄 Paper: https://lnkd.in/dnGxDwdH 💻 Code and benchmark: https://lnkd.in/dUGvTCNF Grateful to work with Mingdai Yang , Duohao Wang, Canyu Chen , Yongfeng Zhang, Hua Wei , Manling Li , Julian McAuley , Kun Zhang, Philip Yu , Colleen(Kejing) Y. , and Zhiwei Liu . #AIAgents #AgenticCommerce #MultiAgentSystems #Benchmark #AgenticEnvironment

Won the intern hackathon at T-Mobile last week alongside my partner, Cooper Hampton . Our team built a full-stack AI benefits navigator to help disabled veterans access the resources they're entitled to, and shipped it in 16 hours. I led the technical build: React frontend, FastAPI backend, and a keyword-scoring NLP layer (alias expansion, intent weighting, conversational context resolution) that routes natural-language queries across 15 different benefit domains with no live model dependency. One thing I had to figure out on the fly: I had four Claude Code agents working in parallel to hit our timeline, which meant setting up file-ownership rules upfront so they wouldn't overwrite each other. It worked, we shipped 15+ components without a single merge conflict, but I spent more time thinking about how to coordinate the agents than writing code myself. We also set hard limits on what the tool could and couldn't say. No eligibility determinations, no tax advice, nothing touching protected-class status, everything scoped to draft-only correspondence so we stayed within 38 CFR Part 14. Felt important to get that right given who the tool is actually for. Got the privilege to present the project to and be judged by a panel of T-Mobile Executives, who voted unanimously to award us first place: Chief Legal Officer Mark Nelson Chief Financial Officer Peter Osvaldik Chief Network Officer Ankur Kapoor Chief Data & AI Officer Grant R. Excited to share that our paper "Comparing Developer and LLM Biases in Code Evaluation" has been accepted to COLM 2026 and the ICML DL4C Workshop! As LLMs are increasingly deployed as judges to evaluate code, a key question remains: Do they actually care about the same things human developers care about? To find out, we introduced TRACE, a framework designed to evaluate LLM judges in realistic, interactive software engineering settings. Key takeaways from our findings: 📉 Alignment Gap: Even the best LLM judges underperform human annotators by 12–23% when predicting developer preferences. 🔍 Systematic Biases: TRACE exposed significant sources of misalignment. For instance, in code completion settings, LLM judges overemphasize functionality, whereas real developers prioritize code clarity. 🛠️ Code Quality Mismatch: The majority of these misalignments map directly to standard software engineering code quality criteria where models and humans weigh priorities completely differently. Huge thank you to Ryan Shar for his collaboration throughout this project! Also deeply grateful to Valerie Chen and Wayne Chi for their guidance, and my collaborators Zichu Wu and Shyam Agarwal . Check out the full preprint on arXiv if you're interested in LLM evaluation in code settings: https://lnkd.in/gD_FDKW9

✨ 𝐀 𝐧𝐞𝐰 𝐭𝐲𝐩𝐞 𝐨𝐟 𝐭𝐨𝐮𝐜𝐡 𝐝𝐚𝐭𝐚 𝐭𝐡𝐚𝐭 𝐦𝐚𝐲 𝐜𝐡𝐚𝐧𝐠𝐞 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝐠𝐚𝐦𝐞 𝐨𝐟 𝐫𝐨𝐛𝐨𝐭𝐢𝐜 𝐝𝐚𝐭𝐚 𝐜𝐨𝐥𝐥𝐞𝐜𝐭𝐢𝐨𝐧. Nearly every tactile sensor today infers contact from surface deformation, and that assumption costs us three ways: it goes blind on 𝐟𝐫𝐚𝐠𝐢𝐥𝐞, 𝐥𝐢𝐪𝐮𝐢𝐝, or 𝐜𝐨𝐦𝐩𝐥𝐢𝐜𝐚𝐭𝐞𝐝 𝐨𝐛𝐣𝐞𝐜𝐭𝐬 right at the moment contact begins; it demands 𝐜𝐚𝐥𝐢𝐛𝐫𝐚𝐭𝐢𝐨𝐧 redone for every mechanical design that may not transfer from one to anther; and the format might not be compatible to vision-language 𝐟𝐨𝐮𝐧𝐝𝐚𝐭𝐢𝐨𝐧 𝐦𝐨𝐝𝐞𝐥s. Today we 🔥 𝐨𝐩𝐞𝐧-𝐬𝐨𝐮𝐫𝐜𝐞 🔥 𝐋𝐢𝐠𝐡𝐭𝐓𝐚𝐜𝐭, our new 𝐑𝐒𝐒 𝟐𝟎𝟐𝟔 paper 🚀 — a visual-tactile fingertip sensor that makes contact 𝐝𝐢𝐫𝐞𝐜𝐭𝐥𝐲 𝐯𝐢𝐬𝐢𝐛𝐥𝐞, no deformation required. Its 𝐚𝐦𝐛𝐢𝐞𝐧𝐭-𝐛𝐥𝐨𝐜𝐤𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐨𝐩𝐭𝐢𝐜𝐚𝐥 𝐝𝐞𝐬𝐢𝐠𝐧 suppresses both external and internal light everywhere except at true contact points, where scattered light leaks through. Contact stops being a 𝐦𝐞𝐜𝐡𝐚𝐧𝐢𝐜𝐚𝐥 inference problem and becomes an 𝐨𝐩𝐭𝐢𝐜𝐚𝐥 fact you can just see. 🔍 What we found: - 𝐍𝐞𝐚𝐫-𝐛𝐥𝐚𝐜𝐤 𝐧𝐨𝐧-𝐜𝐨𝐧𝐭𝐚𝐜𝐭 𝐩𝐢𝐱𝐞𝐥𝐬 (mean gray value < 3) alongside natural-looking contact pixels — robust to material, contact force, surface appearance, and lighting. - Over 𝟗𝟖% 𝐩𝐢𝐱𝐞𝐥-𝐥𝐞𝐯𝐞𝐥 𝐬𝐞𝐠𝐦𝐞𝐧𝐭𝐚𝐭𝐢𝐨𝐧 𝐚𝐜𝐜𝐮𝐫𝐚𝐜𝐲 across diverse materials, with 𝐧𝐨 𝐦𝐢𝐧𝐢𝐦𝐮𝐦 𝐟𝐨𝐫𝐜𝐞 𝐭𝐡𝐫𝐞𝐬𝐡𝐨𝐥𝐝. - Real manipulation tasks that force- and deformation-based sensors fail on: 𝐰𝐚𝐭𝐞𝐫 𝐬𝐩𝐫𝐞𝐚𝐝𝐢𝐧𝐠, 𝐟𝐚𝐜𝐢𝐚𝐥-𝐜𝐫𝐞𝐚𝐦 𝐝𝐢𝐩𝐩𝐢𝐧𝐠, and 𝐭𝐡𝐢𝐧-𝐟𝐢𝐥𝐦 𝐢𝐧𝐭𝐞𝐫𝐚𝐜𝐭𝐢𝐨𝐧. - Spatially aligned visual-tactile images that 𝐕𝐋𝐌𝐬 𝐜𝐚𝐧 𝐫𝐞𝐚𝐝 𝐝𝐢𝐫𝐞𝐜𝐭𝐥𝐲 — e.g., reasoning about resistor color codes for robotic sorting, with no extra calibration model in between. 🤖 Why it matters: as robots move from rigid pick-and-place into delicate, human-shared environments — food handling, skincare, healthcare — the bottleneck is no longer grip strength but 𝐩𝐞𝐫𝐜𝐞𝐢𝐯𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝐥𝐢𝐠𝐡𝐭𝐞𝐬𝐭 𝐭𝐨𝐮𝐜𝐡. Contact you can't sense is contact you can't control. This may trigger a new type of 𝐝𝐚𝐭𝐚 𝐜𝐨𝐥𝐥𝐞𝐜𝐭𝐢𝐨𝐧 for 𝐩𝐮𝐫𝐞𝐥𝐲 𝐯𝐢𝐬𝐢𝐨𝐧-𝐛𝐚𝐬𝐞𝐝 𝐭𝐚𝐜𝐭𝐢𝐥𝐞 𝐬𝐞𝐧𝐬𝐢𝐧𝐠. Because LightTact turns contact into something a camera can directly see, it can automatically stamp the very onset of touch — ground truth that ordinary cameras can then learn to perceive on their own. Paper: https://lnkd.in/gbBAWWFY Project: https://lnkd.in/gTUrNJ62 Code: https://lnkd.in/gipQWEEP This work is co-led by my students Changyi Lin and Boda Huo from Carnegie Mellon University . Thanks to our lab member Mingyang Yu , and collaborators Emily Ruppel , Bingqing Chen , and Jonathan Francis from Bosch . #Robotics #TactileSensing #TouchSensing #Sensors #RobotManipulation #DexterousManipulation #RobotLearning #EmbodiedAI #AI #Humanoids #RSS2026 #Carnegie Carnegie Mellon University #BoschAI

Soon people will realize that we need much more data than we initially thought to reach the “ChatGPT moment” for robots. One key category of missing data is touch. To understand contact-rich dexterous interaction, motion alone is not enough—we also need information about surface properties and contact states. Excited to share 𝐀𝐑𝐓-𝐆𝐥𝐨𝐯𝐞 🚀 , an articulated tactile glove that captures contact-grounded information while preserving full human dexterity. Led by my student Changyi Lin . What ART-Glove provides, all at once: - 𝐊𝐧𝐨𝐰𝐧 𝐠𝐞𝐨𝐦𝐞𝐭𝐫𝐲 — 16 rigid functional surfaces - 𝐒𝐮𝐫𝐟𝐚𝐜𝐞 𝐦𝐨𝐭𝐢𝐨𝐧 — 22 anatomically aligned joints - 𝐓𝐚𝐜𝐭𝐢𝐥𝐞 𝐜𝐨𝐧𝐭𝐚𝐜𝐭 — 2,048 piezoresistive taxels Why this matters: teaching robots to manipulate the way people do requires demonstration data that is physically grounded — not just where the hand moved, but which surfaces touched what, and how. By combining known geometry, articulated motion, and dense tactile sensing in a wearable that doesn't sacrifice dexterity, 𝐀𝐑𝐓-𝐆𝐥𝐨𝐯𝐞 turns ordinary human hands into a rich source of contact-rich manipulation data. Huge congrats to Changyi Lin for leading this work, and thanks to Yuxiang Yang , Maria Bauza Villalonga , Maria Bauza Villalonga , and Peide Huang for the valuable advice and discussions. Paper: arxiv.org/abs/2606.16370 #Robotics #TactileSensing #DexterousManipulation #EmbodiedAI #CMU

TraceRoot.AI (YC S25) now natively traces pi-mono! A few weeks ago Databricks benchmarked coding agents on their own multi-million-line codebase. The surprise winner on cost-efficiency: pi — the minimal, white-box harness from Mario Zechner . Running the same models, it matched the vendor harnesses (Claude Code / Codex) on quality at up to 2× lower cost per task — mostly because it feeds the model ~3× less context per turn: a tighter working set, fewer runs. Honestly, I've been recommending pi to my founder friends for a while now: it's minimal, fully customizable (the whole harness is yours to edit), and you adapt it to your workflow instead of the other way around. If you're building agents, it's worth a serious look. And the moment you host one in your product, observability stops being optional. And now you can see exactly what a pi run is doing with traceroot! 1. CLI extension → if you run pi as a coding agent `pi install npm:@traceroot-ai/pi-extension` Every pi run you kick off from the terminal gets traced automatically — conversation turns, LLM calls, tool executions, cost, tokens. 2. pi SDK wrapper (v0.1.8) → if you build on pi inside your own product When pi is the engine behind your customer-facing agent, wire it in with a few lines: `TraceRoot.initialize({ instrumentModules: { piCodingAgent: pi } })` Traces flow straight to our cloud platform — into CI or any automations. Same rich output either way: per-query traces, planning → every tool call → final output, with the token count on each step — so you can watch where your context budget goes, and see for yourself why pi is so lean. Open source, free tier, a few lines to get going. - pi extension: https://lnkd.in/eMCdkp7W - SDK (v0.1.8): https://lnkd.in/eVnMcV4u Give it a try! 👉 app.traceroot.ai

TraceRoot.AI (YC S25) now has dashboards, purpose-built for AI agents! 📊 Individual traces are perfect for deep dives. But when you want the big picture — latency, cost, tokens, and error rate across all your agents over time — aggregated metrics just belong in a dashboard. So we built one. What's in Dashboard v1: - A seeded Overview dashboard out of the box, so you're never staring at a blank page - A widget builder with live preview — build the charts you want and watch them render as you go - Time-series charts with percentiles, averages, counts, and category breakdowns, over any time range - A trace-feed widget where every row clicks straight through to the actual trace behind the number Coming soon: - Pull your dashboard's aggregated metrics straight from the CLI 🖥️ - Create persistent dashboards from the CLI instead of the UI stay tuned~ 👉 app.traceroot.ai
